Every spider has eight legs..why: Stated explicitly and very often ('spiders have eight legs' 1,795 times in Dolma), and in Wikipedia's Spider article. It could also be derived (spiders are arachnids, arachnids have eight legs), but the direct form is so common that a model holds it directly. The counterfactual occurs in low-quality text (57 hits, sampled: confused children's and pest pages), which makes it plausible.

sources.note: Sampled hits are confused pages (e.g. contrasting spiders with spider crabs or scorpions the wrong way round).

sources.quote: Each of the eight legs of a spider consists of seven distinct parts.

notes: TBox rule edit. Derivability very_unlikely: see evidence. Two determinate queries on new members named in the prompt (the rule is the only route) and two background-belief queries on well-known members whose value a model may store by name. Following the README and the coordinator's ruling, in a world where the stored value wins, the member's spider membership gives way; it never becomes an exception to the edited rule (that would be the inconsistent patch). The two members' storage choices are independent, so four worlds. R1: adult spiders have eight legs with no exceptions at the level of species (injury aside). The near query asks the body parts (two), whose answer differs from the new value. The new members are real, little-known species (Bagheera kiplingi, a herbivorous jumping spider; Eriovixia gryffindori, named after the Sorting Hat); their membership is stated in the prompt.
